description: AYNI ORBITAL is a team driven by collaboration, innovation, and a passion for using space data to serve people. Through NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, we are building an accessible web platform that translates NASA Earth data into sound and touch, so anyone can hear and feel how our planet changes, regardless of vision, hearing, or internet access. We start from the southern Andes of Peru, where water, agriculture, mining, and seismic activity converge.
summary: Pacha Takiy ("the Earth sings" in Quechua) is a lightweight web platform that turns NASA satellite data into sound, vibration and text, so that anyone can hear and feel how a territory changes, including people with visual or hearing disabilities and deafblind people. We chose The Earth Information Jukebox challenge and took it further with haptics, voice control and offline use. Our pilot case is Moquegua, in the southern Andes of Peru, where water, agriculture and mining meet, and where summer rain in the highlands decides a whole year of water. The app pairs NASA Earth Information Center frames (SVS 4285, global precipitation) and NASA GPM IMERG rainfall over Moquegua with sonification generated in real time: rain intensity becomes 2, 4 or 7 tones at 440 Hz, and a background rumble grows with the area covered by rain. Users can listen with a voice guide, see the rain without sound through captions and a visual puddle, or feel every tone as a vibration. Every sound follows one public rule anyone can learn in a minute, checked by automated tests.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Pacha Takiy makes NASA Earth science accessible to everyone, including people with visual, hearing or combined (deafblind) disabilities. It turns NASA rainfall data for Moquegua, Peru, into sound, vibration and captions, synchronized with Earth Information Center frames, following the Earth Jukebox idea: each visual frame is paired with a sonification generated live in the browser.

THREE WAYS TO LIVE THE RAIN

  • Listen: a voice guide leads blind and low-vision users step by step, with hands-free voice control, full keyboard use and screen reader support (NVDA, TalkBack).
  • See: no sound, with synchronized captions, a large visual "puddle" where each tone is seen, and phone vibration, for deaf users.
  • All together: sound, text and vibration at the same time, for classrooms and demonstrations.

HOW IT WORKS (5 steps)

  1. Locate: the user starts with the NASA Earth Information Center global precipitation visualization (SVS 4285), can listen to it region by region, and then zooms into a 1 x 1 degree box around Moquegua (10 x 10 GPM IMERG cells of 0.1 degree).
  2. Learn the sounds: one fixed, public rule. AMS rain intensity classes (light < 2.5 mm/h, moderate 2.5-7.6 mm/h, heavy > 7.6 mm/h) become 2, 4 or 7 tones at 440 Hz in 1.5 s, followed by 1 s of silence. A filtered background rumble grows with the percentage of the area covered by rain. Colors follow the official NASA GIBS legend.
  3. Listen to A and B: two moments with the same intensity differ only by their rain coverage (25.4% vs 12.1%), so the ear learns to hear area.
  4. Reveal: the user compares what they heard with the NASA image and its scale.
  5. Walk through the afternoon: six IMERG frames of 10 Feb 2025, 13:30-16:00, played in sequence.

A separate calm mode plays the NASA data sonification of Caldwell 73 (SVS 13786), the reference for our method: fixed, public rules explained to the listener.

FROM DROUGHT TO FLOW, 3D AND TOUCH & FEEL

  • El Nino mode ("From drought to flow"): 44 rainy seasons (Dec-Mar, 1981-2025) of NASA POWER precipitation (MERRA-2) for the upper basin, played with the same 2/4/7 tones for below-normal, normal and above-normal seasons, with the ocean colored by NOAA's Oceanic Nino Index. 4 of the 5 strong El Nino seasons were below normal. With today's strong El Nino this is relevant now; it is historical evidence, not an official forecast (see ENFEN and SENAMHI).
  • 3D view: the rain falls over the real relief of Moquegua from NASA SRTM, from the Pacific coast to the Ubinas volcano.
  • Touch & Feel for deafblind users: slide a finger through time and feel more pulses for more rain.

COMFORT AND SAFETY

Audio limiter, sound that never overlaps with the voice, no flashes, reduced-motion support and vibration that can be turned off. Most of the app works offline; only the map tiles and the assistant need internet.

VALIDITY

Automated tests check that what sounds is exactly what the rule says (pytest) and that the interface meets accessibility and color contrast checks (Playwright and axe). The real browser audio matches a published mathematical model within 0.17 dB, checked with Sonic Visualiser.

TOOLS

HTML5, JavaScript, Web Audio API, Web Vibration API, Web Speech API, Leaflet, Three.js, Python, pytest, Playwright, axe-core, GitHub Pages, Vercel, Sonic Visualiser, Google Gemini (optional voice assistant "Takiy").

NEXT PHASE

Following our initial proposal: NASA SMAP soil moisture and MODIS/VIIRS vegetation as new sound layers, the "Chacra Sonora" (sound farm field) demo for farmers, and game controller haptics (Gamepad API).

IMPACT

Pacha Takiy lets schools, farmers, local authorities and people with disabilities in Moquegua explore NASA rain data without reading a color map. The method works for any region covered by GPM IMERG.

TEAM

Ayni Orbital, NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, Moquegua local event, Peru. A multidisciplinary team from Food Industry, Mining, Mechanical-Electrical, Telecommunications and Systems Engineering.
